title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
In 1939, surveyors hired by the federal Home Owners’ Loan Corporation graded every neighborhood in Detroit on a four-point scale. Grade A — colored green — meant “best”: new housing stock, “American business and professional men.” Grade D — colored red, the origin of the term redlining — meant “hazardous”: older housing, high Black population, and therefore a poor risk for a federally-backed mortgage (Mitchell & Franco, 2018).
Those grades shaped who could buy a home, build equity, and accumulate wealth over three generations (Aaronson, Hartley & Mazumder, 2021). Grade-D neighborhoods were starved of investment; grade-A suburbs — Grosse Pointe, Birmingham, Royal Oak — were built up with federal dollars, highway access, and restrictive deeds (Rothstein, 2017). When the auto industry contracted after 1970, the pain concentrated where it always had: in the city’s D-grade east and near-east side.
Today Detroit has two bus systems that don’t fully talk to each other. DDOT serves the city; SMART serves the suburbs. For decades there was no unified fare, no seamless transfer. The informal boundary between them traces, with uncomfortable precision, the boundary between the HOLC’s C/D zones and the A/B suburbs to the north.
What follows uses 2022 ACS 5-year estimates to ask whether the 1939 map still predicts who has a car, who takes the bus, and who can afford not to think about either. These are correlations, not causes. But the correlations are worth looking at.

What follows uses 2022 ACS 5-year estimates to ask whether the 1939 map still predicts who has a car, who takes the bus, and who can afford not to think about either. These are correlations, not causes. But the correlations are worth looking at.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
1. Where the lines were drawn
The Mapping Inequality project at the University of Richmond digitized the original HOLC appraisal maps from the National Archives (Nelson et al., 2023). Each polygon below is a neighborhood assessed by a local real estate agent under federal direction in 1939. The tooltips include the original neighborhood name.


Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook


Grade D polygons blanket the near east side, the lower east side, and much of the inner city — the areas home to the bulk of Detroit’s Black population, who had migrated north during and after World War I seeking industrial work. Grade A and B areas extend to the northwest and along the northern edge of the city, toward what would become the white-flight corridor into Oakland County.
What strikes you looking at the map is how geometric the logic was. The 8 Mile Road boundary and the Grosse Pointe city limits weren’t just municipal lines — they were where the grades changed, and where federal mortgage credit started and stopped.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
2. Car access by HOLC grade
In a metro region where transit is fragmented and job sprawl is severe, car access is not a lifestyle preference. A household without a car in the Detroit metro has limited access to the suburban job centers that now hold most of the region’s employment. The question is whether the historical grade still predicts who has a car today.









The gradient runs in the expected direction: grade-D tracts have the highest median share of car-free households, grade-A the lowest. But the spread within each grade is wide, particularly in grade D. That internal variation may reflect pockets of gentrification, areas with unusually good transit coverage, or the coarseness of assigning a single 1939 grade to a 2022 census tract.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
3. Who rides the bus
High transit use in a car-dependent region can mean two different things: genuine preference, or constrained necessity. The ACS tells us what people do, not why. Still, if transit commuting is concentrated in historically redlined tracts, it raises a question about whether the infrastructure serving those tracts is commensurate with the demand.









Transit use does climb from A to D, but that gradient exists within a region where the overall transit commute share is low — Detroit is still, structurally, a car city. The deeper question: are the bus routes serving grade-D tracts frequent enough and geographically comprehensive enough to reach suburban employment centers? DDOT and SMART have historically operated as separate systems with limited cross-boundary service (SEMCOG), a structural feature that the commute-share data surfaces but cannot explain.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
4. The economic gradient
The HOLC grades were, explicitly, an economic instrument — they determined access to federally-backed mortgage credit, the primary mechanism for building household wealth in postwar America. Eighty years later, the income and poverty gradient across the same geography is still legible.









The income gradient is steep and consistent. This is not surprising — it’s roughly what the redlining literature has documented nationally (Aaronson, Hartley & Mazumder, 2021). But the Detroit case has particular features: the collapse of the auto industry accelerated decline in areas that were already disinvested, and racial exclusion from the suburbs was enforced not just by HOLC grades but by deed covenants, blockbusting, and the deliberate routing of I-75 and I-94 through Black neighborhoods in the 1950s and 60s (Rothstein, 2017).
The gradient is real. The mechanism is overdetermined. HOLC grades may be one thread among several, not the whole story.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
5. The geography of car access
The box plots above summarize distributions by grade, but the spatial pattern matters on its own. Where exactly are the car-free households, and do they cluster in ways that overlap the 1939 boundary lines?


Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook


The darkest areas — highest car-free rates — cluster in the inner city, overlapping the red-outlined grade-D polygons. The gradient is not perfectly clean: some grade-C tracts show high car-free rates, and suburban grade-A areas have near-zero rates. But the spatial coincidence is striking enough to motivate the next chart.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
6. The compounding trap
Low income limits car access. Low car access limits job access. Job access limits income. The scatter below asks whether this trap clusters in the areas that the HOLC graded as hazardous.









Grade-D points cluster toward the upper-left quadrant: low income, high car-free rate. Grade-A points cluster lower-right. The clustering is not absolute — there is overlap between grades, and some grade-D tracts have incomes and car-access rates closer to the metro median, likely reflecting ongoing neighborhood change. But the center of gravity of each grade is where you would expect it if the 1939 map were still doing work.
This is a cross-sectional snapshot. It cannot tell us whether redlining caused this clustering, or whether the same underlying forces that shaped the 1939 grades are still at work through other mechanisms.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
section: 8. Bus stop access across HOLC grades
text:
8. Bus stop access across HOLC grades
The transit commute share in §3 reflects revealed behavior — who actually rides. But it cannot tell us whether the infrastructure is there to use. Two more basic questions: Is there a bus stop within a 5-minute walk of a typical resident in each grade zone? And if so, how often does that bus actually come?
We use OpenStreetMap stop locations queried via the Overpass API — covering both DDOT and SMART — for the proximity question, and SMART GTFS schedule data for frequency. DDOT’s GTFS feed is not publicly accessible, so the frequency picture is partial: SMART primarily serves the suburbs, meaning grades A and B have better frequency coverage in this data. That bias is worth keeping in mind.





























Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook


The bus-stop geography inverts the intuition you might carry from the economic and car-access charts. Because Detroit’s inner city is the densest part of the metro, it actually has relatively high stop density — grade-D tracts are often within a short walk of a DDOT stop. The suburban grade-A and grade-B zones, built around the automobile, have sparser stop networks and longer walk distances.
But proximity alone is not service. The SMART GTFS data shows that in the outer-ring zones — where stops do exist — they come infrequently. The compounding problem for grade-D residents runs in the opposite direction: stops are nearby, but the ACS commute data suggests transit use remains constrained even where stops are present. The most likely explanation is not stop proximity but network reach: a dense stop network that loops within a neighborhood is not the same as one that connects reliably to suburban employment centers.
The most important missing piece is a job-accessibility isochrone — how many jobs can a resident reach by transit within 45 minutes? That would require GTFS from both agencies and an origin-destination travel-time matrix. The LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES) provide the employment side of this equation; the transit side remains unavailable in a public, consolidated format for this region.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
section: 7. What the data can’t tell us
text:
7. What the data can’t tell us
On transit adequacy. The ACS tells us who takes transit; it doesn’t tell us whether transit goes where people need it to go. The bus stop analysis in §8 is a first pass. What’s still missing: what share of grade-D tract residents are within walking distance of a route with 30-minute or better headways? That would require GTFS from both agencies layered onto this spatial analysis.
On job accessibility. Car-free rate is only a problem if the jobs reachable without a car are insufficient. A follow-on analysis using LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES) could calculate the number of jobs reachable within 45 minutes by transit for each tract — a much sharper mobility indicator than commute mode share.
On displacement and change. These are 2022 tracts on a 1939 map. Corktown — historically grade C/D, adjacent to the Ford-backed Michigan Central Station development — is changing rapidly. The snapshot doesn’t capture whether the residents who benefit from infrastructure investment are the same people who bore the costs of disinvestment.
On causation. The correlations here are consistent with HOLC grades having long-run effects on neighborhood outcomes (Aaronson, Hartley & Mazumder, 2021). They are also consistent with explanations that have little to do with the HOLC maps themselves: racial exclusion enforced through private deed covenants, federal highway routing that severed Black neighborhoods from job centers, blockbusting by real estate agents (Rothstein, 2017). Disentangling these mechanisms would require something like a regression discontinuity design — comparing tracts on either side of a grade boundary that were otherwise similar in 1939.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
section: A note on method and data
text:
A note on method and data
The grade assigned to each census tract reflects whichever HOLC grade covered the largest share of the tract’s area within HOLC-surveyed territory, provided that share was at least 60%. Tracts where no single grade dominated are excluded from the grade-stratified charts but retained in the maps. The 60% threshold is a judgment call; at 50% or 70% the counts change but the directional pattern does not.
ACS 5-year 2022 estimates smooth year-to-year noise but can mask rapid recent change. Tract-level averages obscure within-tract variation, which can be substantial in larger or heterogeneous tracts. Census tract boundaries were retrieved via pygris. Bus stop locations are from OpenStreetMap (queried Overpass API, March 2026) and cover stops tagged as highway=bus_stop or public_transport=stop_position within the three-county metro area. Transit frequency reflects SMART GTFS only; DDOT GTFS is not publicly available.
The gradient documented here is real. The mechanism is a question — one that the data motivates but does not resolve.

Data sources

HOLC neighborhood boundaries: Mapping Inequality, Digital Scholarship Lab, University of Richmond.
ACS 5-year 2022 estimates: U.S. Census Bureau.
Census tract boundaries: pygris (TIGER/Line 2022).
Bus stop locations: OpenStreetMap contributors via Overpass API.
Transit schedules: SMART GTFS (retrieved March 2026).

References

Aaronson, D., Hartley, D., & Mazumder, B. (2021). The effects of the 1930s HOLC ‘redlining’ maps on CD outcomes. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 13(4), 355–392. doi:10.1257/pol.20190414
Mitchell, B., & Franco, J. (2018). HOLC ‘Redlining’ Maps: The persistent structure of segregation and economic inequality. NCRC. ncrc.org/holc
Nelson, R. K., Winling, L., Marciano, R., & Connolly, N. (2023). Mapping Inequality: Redlining in New Deal America. American Panorama, University of Richmond. dsl.richmond.edu/panorama/redlining
Rothstein, R. (2017). The Color of Law: A Forgotten History of How Our Government Segregated America. Liveright/Norton. wwnorton.com

title: Do Festival Lineups Follow a Network?
text: This project investigates whether the artists who share festival stages form a network with real, measurable structure, structure strong enough to predict who else an artist is likely to play with, and whether that structure is explained by the music itself or by something else entirely. Festival lineups are expensive, high-stakes decisions: promoters spend months assembling artists to balance genre, audience draw, and cost, largely on the strength of relationships and industry intuition rather than data [1]. A co-performance network, where two artists are linked whenever they share a festival bill, offers a way to test that intuition directly. Built from 2023 lineups at 30 U.S. and international festivals and supplemented with Spotify’s track-level audio features, this project asks two questions: does the structure of who-plays-with-whom carry enough signal to predict connections the model hasn’t seen, and can that same structure be explained by what the artists actually sound like?

title: Do Festival Lineups Follow a Network?
text:
Building the Network
Nodes in the network are individual artists; an edge connects two artists whenever they performed at the same festival, weighted by how many festivals they shared. Lineups came from official festival posters, most of which exist only as promotional images, so artist names were extracted with Google’s Gemini model and manually validated to correct OCR errors and remove hallucinated entries. Artist metadata, danceability, energy, tempo, valence, genre, and popularity, came from a companion Spotify tracks dataset, matched to the network’s artist list.
The resulting graph has 3,729 artists and 507,144 edges. It is a single snapshot of the 2023 festival circuit, and it skews heavily toward electronic dance music: EDM festivals account for roughly 37% of the sample, since most large festivals run a dedicated EDM stage or night even when their overall billing is genre-diverse. That skew matters for how the community-detection results below should be read.

title: Do Festival Lineups Follow a Network?
text:
Network Structure: Small-World, Not Random


{'diameter': 4, 'avg_shortest_path': 2.2830746313835304, 'avg_degree': 272.31536604987934, 'avg_clustering_coeff': 0.9236414851854906}




Density: 0.07304596728805776











A diameter of 4 and an average shortest path of 2.28 mean that almost any two of the network’s 3,729 artists are connected through two or three shared festivals, and the clustering coefficient of 0.92 says that artists who share one festival-mate tend to share several more. That combination, short paths and dense local clustering, is the signature of a small-world network.
To check whether that structure was anything more than what density alone would produce, the network was compared against a Watts-Strogatz random-rewiring model matched on node count, edge count, and average degree (Table 1). Even at zero rewiring probability, the Watts-Strogatz model tops out at a clustering coefficient of 0.75, well below the network’s observed 0.92, so the real network is meaningfully more clustered than a comparably-sized lattice. Its assortativity coefficient of 0.313 adds another piece to that picture: well-connected artists tend to co-perform with other well-connected artists, a pattern familiar from real-world collaboration networks such as scientific co-authorship.

title: Do Festival Lineups Follow a Network?
text:
Communities Within the Network









To find substructure inside the larger network, two community-detection algorithms were compared on 10%-node subgraph samples: Louvain modularity optimization and Girvan-Newman edge-betweenness partitioning. Louvain consistently produced tighter, larger communities across every sampled subgraph (modularity Q = 0.66 on one representative sample, versus Q = 0.25 for Girvan-Newman) and was adopted for the full analysis. Girvan-Newman turned out to be a poor fit for this particular network: because the graph is small-world, with an average shortest path of only 2.28, there are many alternate routes between any two artists, so no single edge acts as an obvious bridge for betweenness to detect.
Applying Louvain modularity to the full network, rather than a sample, surfaced 11 distinct communities at a modularity score of 0.60, a strong division for a network this dense. Community sizes range widely, from 948 artists in the largest to 62 in the smallest, which already hints that these clusters are not simply “genre buckets” of equal size.

title: Do Festival Lineups Follow a Network?
section: The Festivals That Hold It Together
text:
The Festivals That Hold It Together
A natural follow-up question: how much of that structure is being driven by a handful of dominant festivals? Modularity clustering was re-run using only the artists who performed at Lollapalooza, Austin City Limits, and Coachella, arguably the three highest-profile U.S. festivals in the dataset.










How far does the reach of the big three extend?
Artists who played Lollapalooza, Coachella, or Austin City Limits in 2023 also turned up in roughly 27 of the other 30 festivals in the dataset, domestic and international. No single community from this clustering was confined to just one of the three festivals, so the overlap looks less like three separate artist pools and more like a shared touring circuit that these festivals sit at the center of. A closer read of two of the resulting communities is suggestive without being conclusive: one skewed toward pop headliners, another toward rock and alternative acts, which points to genre as one organizing factor among several, alongside geography and booking relationships.

title: Do Festival Lineups Follow a Network?
section: Testing the Structure With Link Prediction
text:
Testing the Structure With Link Prediction
Community structure is descriptive; it says the network is organized, not that the organization is useful. To test whether the structure carries real predictive signal, link prediction was framed around one smaller festival, Sunburn, and evaluated under three scenarios designed to avoid the leakage that would come from training and testing on the same festival’s edges.
Case 1 tried to predict links within Sunburn’s own lineup, using only past co-performance data. Case 2 predicted links from Sunburn’s artists out to every other festival’s performers, with Sunburn’s own edges withheld from training. Case 3 ran the same out-of-festival prediction, but kept the edges belonging to the three major U.S. festivals (Lollapalooza, Coachella, Austin City Limits) in the training graph.

The pattern across all three cases points the same direction. Case 1 collapsed on precision (0.008) despite near-perfect recall, because intra-festival connections are so sparse that almost any predicted pair is a false positive. Case 2, shown in the confusion matrix above, was more conservative: moderate precision (0.815) but recall low enough (0.175) that most real Sunburn-to-elsewhere connections went undetected. Case 3 is the standout: with the major festivals’ edges left in the training graph, the model predicted Sunburn’s external connections almost perfectly (F1 = 0.979, AUC = 0.999). The major festivals are acting as structural anchors, once the model can see how an artist relates to Lollapalooza, Coachella, or Austin City Limits, its connections to the rest of the network become highly predictable. Remove that anchor and prediction degrades sharply. That is strong evidence that a small set of festivals disproportionately shapes the topology of the entire touring circuit.

title: Do Festival Lineups Follow a Network?
section: Does the Music Explain the Communities?
text:
Does the Music Explain the Communities?
The second research question flips the first one around: given that Louvain found 11 communities in the network, are those communities separable by what the artists actually sound like, or by genre? If booking patterns tracked musical similarity, community membership should be at least somewhat predictable from Spotify’s audio features (danceability, energy, tempo, valence, and similar) and genre metadata.

None of the four came close to reliable classification; logistic regression’s 24.9% was the best of a weak field, against a naive baseline of roughly 9% for 11 balanced classes, real but modest signal. The likely explanation is homogeneity rather than randomness: every community, regardless of its position in the network, is dominated by EDM sub-genres and EDM-heavy festivals. Community 1, for instance, is built mostly from artists in minimal techno, hardstyle, drum-and-bass, dub, and house, who mainly performed at EDM-focused festivals like Tomorrowland and EDC, but also turn up at nearly every other festival in the dataset. When every community shares a similar genre mix, genre stops being a useful axis for telling them apart, even though it may still shape the network at a coarser level.

title: Do Festival Lineups Follow a Network?
text:
Conclusion
Structurally, the 2023 festival circuit behaves like a small-world network: short paths, dense local clustering, and a handful of major festivals, Lollapalooza, Austin City Limits, Coachella, acting as hubs that connect otherwise-separate regional and genre-based touring circuits. That structure is not just descriptive; it is predictive, link prediction anchored on those major festivals reconstructed a smaller festival’s outside connections with near-perfect accuracy. What the network’s structure does not explain is the music itself: the 11 communities Louvain found were not meaningfully separable by audio features or genre, which suggests that co-performance is driven less by how artists sound and more by relationships, geography, and the logistics of who tours where. The circuit runs on connections, and a small number of central festivals hold a disproportionate amount of the network together.

title: Do Festival Lineups Follow a Network?
text:
Limitations
The dataset is a single-year (2023) snapshot, which rules out any analysis of how the network evolves year over year, and it is heavily skewed toward EDM festivals, which likely inflates the apparent lack of musical separability between communities. The network also lacks the business-side metadata, record labels, promoter and agency affiliations, radius clauses limiting how close together an artist can play, that plausibly explain co-performance patterns better than either network topology or musical similarity can. Extending the dataset across multiple years, and incorporating that business context, would be the natural next step for testing whether these findings generalize beyond 2023.

title: Predicting Inflammatory Bowel Disease from Survey Data
text: This project investigates how far machine learning can go in flagging a rare chronic condition, inflammatory bowel disease, from routine health-survey responses, and what that predictive ceiling reveals about the limits of survey-based screening. Using two years (2023 and 2024) of National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) data, this project treats severe IBD as fundamentally a class-imbalance problem before it is a feature-engineering one: IBD is rare enough in the general population that a model predicting “no IBD” for every respondent would already score deceptively well on plain accuracy.

title: Predicting Inflammatory Bowel Disease from Survey Data
section: What Separates IBD and Non-IBD Respondents?
text:
What Separates IBD and Non-IBD Respondents?
The first step was descriptive: which survey variables actually differ between respondents who report severe IBD (IBDSEV_A = 1) and those who don’t?
















Comparing response rates between the two groups surfaced five variables with the largest gaps: a history of arthritis (ARTHEV_A), having received a pneumococcal vaccine (SHTPNUEV_A), any prescription use in the past 12 months (RX12M_A), a reported health condition (HLTHCOND_A), and social or work limitations (SOCWRKLIM_A). Most of the strongest discriminators cluster around chronic-disease comorbidity and healthcare utilization rather than demographics, which tracks with what’s already known about IBD: it rarely travels alone. Depression (DEPEV_A) and anxiety (ANXEV_A) were both more common among IBD respondents, plausibly reflecting the psychological weight of a chronic, unpredictable gastrointestinal condition, and so were frequent prescription use and overnight hospital stays (HOSPONGT_A), consistent with the ongoing medical management severe IBD requires. Employment-related variables ran the other way: respondents without IBD were slightly more likely to report currently working or receiving wage income, a pattern consistent with chronic illness limiting employment and income activity, though it’s suggestive here rather than something this analysis can pin down causally.









A correlation matrix across the retained binary features showed the same comorbidity story from a different angle. Depression and anxiety were strongly positively correlated with each other, as expected for conditions that frequently co-occur. Reported health condition (HLTHCOND_A) and immune-suppressing prescription use (MEDRXTRT_A) were highly correlated too, consistent with sicker respondents being more likely to be on immunosuppressive treatment. And the employment-related features, ever worked for an employer, worked last week, wage income, clustered tightly with each other, which is unsurprising since they’re really different facets of the same underlying employment status.

title: Predicting Inflammatory Bowel Disease from Survey Data
text:
Why Simple Separation Doesn’t Work









Projecting the feature set into two principal components made the modeling challenge visible before a single classifier was trained. Respondents with and without IBD were heavily intermixed across the PCA space, with no region where one class predominated without substantial overlap from the other. That means the strongest linear combinations of these features, the ones that explain the most variance in the data, don’t line up with the boundary that actually separates the two classes. Any classifier drawing a decision boundary in this reduced space would struggle, particularly for the minority IBD-positive class. That’s not surprising for a rare chronic condition inferred from a general-purpose health survey rather than clinical data, but it’s worth confirming directly before trusting downstream model results.

title: Predicting Inflammatory Bowel Disease from Survey Data
text:
Modeling an Imbalanced, Rare Outcome
Because severe IBD cases are rare, a model that predicts “no IBD” for everyone would score misleadingly well on accuracy while catching zero real cases. Eight classifiers, two dummy baselines, logistic regression, KNN, an MLP, random forest, random forest with bagging, and XGBoost, were each evaluated under three resampling regimes: no resampling (class weighting only), random undersampling, and SMOTE oversampling. Evaluation used 5-fold TimeSeriesSplit cross-validation to preserve the chronological order between the 2023 and 2024 survey years, with all preprocessing done inside pipelines to avoid leakage, and F1 score, rather than accuracy, as the primary metric.

The results bear out the accuracy warning directly: both dummy baselines scored an F1 of 0.033 to 0.049, better than zero only because of how F1 is computed, and every real model beat them, but not by a wide margin. Logistic regression was the most stable performer across all three regimes (F1 of 0.121 baseline, 0.124 with SMOTE, 0.122 with undersampling) and the best model overall in two of the three. Undersampling helped the weaker models the most: random forest with bagging nearly doubled its F1 (0.079 to 0.125), and the MLP roughly doubled (0.059 to 0.119). XGBoost showed the opposite pattern, it was competitive at baseline (0.108) but degraded under both undersampling (0.078) and SMOTE (0.089), suggesting it was already extracting what signal existed from the untouched class distribution and that resampling mostly added noise. No single model or resampling strategy solved the underlying problem; F1 scores stayed in the 0.05-to-0.13 range across the board, a ceiling set by how little separates the two classes in feature space, not by which algorithm was used.









Feature importances from the fitted models lined up with the earlier discriminator analysis: arthritis history, frequent prescription use, and the mental-health comorbidities (depression and anxiety) were consistently ranked among the strongest predictors across models. That consistency is the most clinically meaningful result of the analysis: even where predictive performance was modest, the models converged on the same real, clinically sensible signal that IBD overlaps heavily with other chronic conditions rather than presenting in isolation.

title: Predicting Inflammatory Bowel Disease from Survey Data
text:
Conclusion
No model or resampling strategy fully solved the class-imbalance problem here. IBD-positive respondents didn’t separate cleanly in feature space, PCA showed heavy overlap between classes, and F1 scores across every approach tested stayed modest. But the exercise surfaced a real signal: arthritis, frequent prescription use, and mental-health comorbidities were consistently the strongest predictors, consistent with IBD’s well-documented pattern of overlapping chronic conditions. The larger lesson was methodological rather than algorithmic: for rare-disease prediction from survey data, feature selection, evaluation-metric choice, and honest accounting for class imbalance matter more than which classifier gets used.

title: Predicting Inflammatory Bowel Disease from Survey Data
text:
Limitations
NHIS is self-reported survey data, not clinical diagnosis, so the target variable reflects what respondents reported rather than a confirmed medical record, and the severity threshold (severe ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s specifically) excludes mild and moderate IBD cases entirely. The two-year window (2023-2024) is also short for a chronic, low-prevalence condition, and the demographic features (race, region, education) necessarily collapse real heterogeneity into broad categories. None of this invalidates the comorbidity signal the models converged on, but it does mean the resulting F1 scores describe a ceiling for this data and this approach, not a ceiling for IBD prediction generally.

title: American national park visits: location density and visitation rates
text:
This project investigates whether the spatial distribution of U.S. national parks influences how often they are visited. The central question is intuitive but surprisingly under-examined: do parks that sit near other parks benefit from that proximity?
For this project, our claim is that American National Parks visitation rates are higher in regions where national parks are geographically closer together, suggesting travelers are more likely to visit multiple parks within a dense cluster.
Three guiding questions structure the analysis:
This hypothesis is based on the intuitive assumption that geographic proximity facilitates multi-park trips, potentially through reduced travel costs, shared infrastructure, and the ability to visit multiple destinations in a single vacation. If correct, we would expect tightly clustered parks to show higher per-park visitation rates than regions with widely dispersed parks.

title: American national park visits: location density and visitation rates
text:
Data choices and justifications
Our first significant data choice was calculating the distances between the parks in each region. As the class dataset did not include geographical data, we decided to import an external dataset and matched parks by name to merge the data. After some light data cleaning to remove duplicates and standardize park names, we utilized the latitude and longitude in the Haversine Formula to calculate the distance between all pairs of parks across regions. We chose to use this formula due to its ability to calculate distances across a sphere using these coordinates accurately, as mentioned in the educational data science site GeeksForGeeks.
Additionally, after finding the Haversine distance between each park, we used a multiplier of 1.4 on each value to account for the variations in road structures (as the distances between each park are likely not straight lines). According to a study published in the National Library of Medicine titled “A Nationwide Comparison of Driving Distance Versus Straight-Line Distance to Hospitals”, in nearly “all locations within the United States,” applying a detour index of about 1.4 to the “straight-line distance” is an “adequate proxy for travel distance”. Though this does not account for more severe detours or uncrossable geographic features (roadblocks, lakes, rivers, etc.), we thought it was a good first step to take to approximate the distance (in miles).
Finally, among our three approaches (discussed below in more detail), one approach involved investigating whether parks closer to metropolitan areas showed any changes in visitation compared to more remote areas. To do this, we used the US Metro Areas Database, which contains coordinates and population data. Then, for each metro area, we used the same Haversine distance calculation to calculate its distance between all parks, only keeping the parks that were within a 300-mile radius of a metro area to ensure we only examined parks that were reasonably accessible from major metropolitan cities (and minimizing any potential bias, such as parks with very low visits or that were remote).

title: American national park visits: location density and visitation rates
text:
Approaches
We used three complementary spatial approaches to test our hypothesis at different scales.

Approach 1: neighbor count
For this approach, we used a pairwise distance calculation, combined with a Pearson Correlation (r) analysis, to test the relationship between park clustering and visitation at an individual park level. For neighbor counting, we defined a spatial radius of 300 miles, which is roughly a 4–6 hour drive. For each park, we counted the number of other parks within this radius and grouped the parks into categories: Isolated (0), Few (1–2), Some (3–5), and Many (6+) neighbors. In addition to calculating the correlation (r) based on the neighbor count (independent variable) and the total recreation visits for each park (dependent variable), we explored the visitation distributions across these categories through summary statistics and box plots.


Approach 2: grid-based analysis
For this approach, we used geographical binning (as well as per-park normalization and correlation analysis to minimize any effects regional distribution may have had) to test clustering effects at a tighter spatial scale. To do this, we divided the U.S. into a grid (we chose 150 by 150 miles, roughly) and converted the grid size from miles to degrees, approximated using 1 degree ≈ 69 miles for both latitude and longitude. While this created some distortion at higher latitudes, most parks fell within similar latitude bands, minimizing the effect.
For each grid square, we calculated park count, total visits, and average visit per park (total visits divided by park count). Without this normalization, grids with more parks would automatically have higher total visits. By averaging visits per park, the analysis isolates the effect of density rather than just quantity.
To have meaningful clustering comparisons, we also only counted the grids that contained at least two parks. We calculated r based on the number of parks in each grid (our independent variable) and the average visits per park in that grid (dependent variable).


Approach 3: metro areas
For each metropolitan area, we identified all parks within a radius and calculated park count near that metro, total visits from all nearby parks, and average visits per park. This normalization was, again, essential, as metros surrounded by many parks should not automatically appear as more “successful” simply because they had more parks within their radius. By normalizing to average visits per park, we were able to test whether individual parks near clustered metro areas receive more visits than parks near metro areas with fewer park options, potentially due to shared tourism infrastructure or marketing.
This approach also allowed us to examine whether metro population size correlates with park visitation, helping distinguish between clustering effects and general urban accessibility effects.

For our grid-based approach, we found a strong, positive correlation between park proximity and the number of visits. From the 54 grids we created, only seven grids had more than two parks — five grids had two parks, and two grids had three parks. When we increase the threshold from 150 to 300 miles, for example, we get 14 grid squares with more than two parks and one grid square with five parks. The correlation then becomes −0.105, suggesting that at an even slightly broader threshold, the clustering “benefits” for visitations disappear. text:
Conclusion
Our hypothesis that geographic clustering increases park visitation is context-dependent. At the broad spatial scale (300-mile radius), clustering shows no effect (r = 0.020), suggesting individual park characteristics dominate visitation decisions. However, within tight geographic clusters (150-mile grids), we DO observe a very strong positive relationship (r = 0.934), indicating that when parks are “truly” close, multi-park tourism does boost visitation. This suggests a distance threshold: parks must be within day-trip distance (~150 miles) for clustering benefits to materialize.

title: American national park visits: location density and visitation rates
text:
Viability of claim
Due to our choices of aggregating park visitations and normalizing across regions in our grid-based analysis, we cannot easily generalize our claim. Particularly with our aggregation — because we focus on total park visits, rather than investigating visitation types or seasonal patterns, our ability to conclude why specific parks receive a certain level of visitors is limited. Our inclusion of a distance threshold also means our findings are mainly applicable to densely clustered parks, rather than those spread out over larger areas. However, we can still evaluate the broader structural relationship between average visitation numbers and the distribution of parks within regions.
Despite these limitations, we do believe the main pattern in our claim would hold in the future. The general trend identified that tightly clustered parks (specifically, within 150 miles of one another) would see higher average visits and would likely remain the same. The number of visits to parks in a region will not solely depend on their proximity to one another; other factors (such as accessibility, tourism, marketing, isolated regions, or climate) will remain factors. The geographic structure of the park regions and surrounding population density will stay stable over time.
If this claim were to hold for other types of parks, it would likely depend on whether the other park systems had a similar geographic clustering and the feasibility of traveling. For example, in other parks that were laid out in a similar way to the national parks (e.g., regions with many parks in proximity that could be realistically visited in a single trip), using proximity to investigate visitation rates will likely be fruitful. For park systems with fewer parks or that are more geographically isolated, proximity is unlikely to correlate to an increase in visitation rates on its own. Future work to ensure our claim is more broadly applicable (as mentioned above) would include integrating temporal analysis and visitation type.

title: Exploring U.S. Airfare Trends
text:
Nominal vs. inflation-adjusted airfare, 1995–2025










Findings
The dual-line chart above shows the central tension of modern air travel that we’re examining: the perceived cost versus the real, inflation-adjusted value. While the Current Dollar (Nominal) Fare (the red line) shows a general upward trend (often giving travelers the impression that flights are constantly getting more expensive), the Inflation-Adjusted Fare (the green line) tells a different story: Despite episodic spikes, the real cost of flying has declined significantly over the past three decades. Using Q1 1995 as a benchmark, the long-term trend shows a major decrease in what an airfare ticket costs relative to other consumer goods. This shows the impact of deregulation and increasing competition from low-cost carriers.
The chart also illustrates how major external shocks interrupt the long-term decline. We examined:

9/11 Attacks (2001): The initial drop in demand caused fares to plunge.
2008 Oil Crisis: This caused the most acute spike outside of the pandemic. As fuel costs hit record highs, the inflation-adjusted fare surged, forcing airlines to pass the expense directly to consumers.
COVID-19 Pandemic (2020): Fares cratered to a historic low, demonstrating that even rock-bottom prices couldn’t entice travelers during the global shutdown.

The overall takeaway for the traveler is that the cost of flying is not steadily increasing; it is an economic roller coaster where long-term affordability is periodically interrupted by massive, yet brief, external shocks.


Airfare over time with year filter










Average airfare by city, 1995
Highlight individual cities to compare fares.









Quarter-over-quarter airfare change during COVID-19, 2018–2022
Measuring and visualizing quarter-over-quarter percentage changes to highlight the magnitude and volatility of price shocks during the pandemic period.










Findings
The most interesting feature of the chart is the deep-red bar corresponding to the second quarter of 2020 (Q2 2020). This bar represents the largest quarterly decline in average domestic airfare in the dataset’s history. The average domestic airfare dropped by approximately 19.8% in Q2 2020 compared to Q1 2020. This is the quarter when most travel restrictions were enacted. Following the massive negative spike, the chart shows a pattern of extreme volatility, characterized by alternating large green (positive) and red (negative) bars in 2021 and 2022. This is possibly due to the market’s erratic attempts to find a new equilibrium as demand pulsed back and forth. The bars representing the years 2018 and 2019 are relatively small and centered around the zero line, demonstrating the pre-pandemic stability of the market. The dramatic scale of the 2020 drop and subsequent rebound starkly highlights the event as an unprecedented external shock to the airline economy.











Airfare and jet fuel prices, 1995–present








This visualization shows how closely domestic airfares have tracked jet fuel prices over the past 30 years—and where that relationship has broken down. In the early years of the series, when fuel was cheap and relatively stable, airfares clustered tightly as well, reflecting a period of intense airline competition and steady consumer demand. The path then swings sharply to the right in the mid-2000s, during the global oil shock, when jet fuel prices surged far faster than ticket prices—evidence that airlines absorbed much of the hit through fees, capacity cuts, and operational changes rather than passing the full cost to travelers. The steep downward drop marks the COVID-19 collapse, when both fuel costs and fares plunged simultaneously to record lows. And on the far right edge, the line bends upward again during the 2022–23 rebound, as high fuel prices and a surge in post-pandemic travel pushed fares to their highest levels in years. Taken together, the chart reveals a long-term dance between fuel costs and ticket prices, punctuated by economic shocks that pull the two series apart before they fall back into step.

title: Health and Poverty Across US Counties
text: This project investigates how closely poverty tracks with health outcomes across U.S. counties, and whether that relationship holds up once the analysis moves past a single state to a national, statistically tested comparison. Starting from Michigan and then merging CDC PLACES county-level health data, over 120,000 county-level health records, with Census American Community Survey (ACS) poverty and income estimates across 3,221 counties, this project asks three questions: does poverty rate meaningfully predict chronic-disease prevalence, which health risk behaviors and racial disparities travel alongside that relationship, and do counties and states naturally sort into distinct health-poverty profiles without being told the answer in advance?

title: Health and Poverty Across US Counties
text:
Setting a Baseline in Michigan









Before scaling up nationally, the analysis started close to home. Michigan’s county-level median household income clusters between roughly $55,000 and $70,000, with a visible tail at both ends: a handful of counties fall below $50,000, and a few climb above $90,000. That spread previewed the pattern the national analysis would later confirm at scale: income variation across counties is real, and it is not evenly distributed.

title: Health and Poverty Across US Counties
section: Does Poverty Predict Health Outcomes Nationwide?
text:
Does Poverty Predict Health Outcomes Nationwide?
Moving beyond Michigan, the full CDC PLACES and Census ACS datasets were merged nationally and tested for whether poverty rate meaningfully predicts each health outcome.









Across the full national dataset, four chronic conditions rose consistently with county poverty rate: obesity, high blood pressure, diabetes, and stroke. Of the six outcomes tested, stroke’s relationship to poverty was the steepest and the most statistically pronounced, an analysis of variance across low-, medium-, and high-poverty counties put stroke’s F-statistic at 1,619.59, ahead of coronary heart disease (1,194.28), diabetes (1,176.48), high blood pressure (1,105.12), COPD (1,004.79), and arthritis (693.80). Cancer (non-skin or melanoma) was the outlier: it showed a weak, slightly negative relationship to poverty rather than the positive one every other condition displayed.









A correlation breakdown across the same six outcomes confirmed the pattern: nearly every chronic condition, arthritis, obesity, high cholesterol, high blood pressure, diabetes, correlated positively with poverty rate at a moderate-to-strong level (0.3 to 0.7). Depression correlated more weakly (around 0.2), suggesting mental-health outcomes are shaped by more than income alone. Cancer was the single negative correlation in the set, a pattern that likely says as much about screening and diagnostic access as it does about underlying disease risk: lower-poverty counties may simply catch and report more cancer, not have less of it.

title: Health and Poverty Across US Counties
text:
Risk Behaviors and Racial Disparities
The analysis also looked at health risk behaviors (smoking, inactivity, sleep, and similar) and at how the poverty-health relationship differs across racial groups.









Health risk behaviors followed a similarly legible pattern. Smoking correlated strongly with COPD and other respiratory disease, consistent with the well-established biological link. Physical inactivity and short sleep duration also correlated positively with several chronic conditions, suggesting sedentary lifestyles and poor sleep compound the same risk. Binge drinking broke the pattern: its correlations with health outcomes were weak or negative, plausibly because binge drinking is more common in wealthier counties with better healthcare access, though confirming that would require controlling for confounders, like alcohol-specific diseases, that this dataset doesn’t capture.
Breaking the poverty-health relationship out by race surfaced a sharper picture within the Hispanic or Latino population specifically: Mississippi shows consistently worse outcomes than Alaska across arthritis, COPD, obesity, high blood pressure, and depression, along with more tooth loss, a proxy for economic barriers to dental care, and wider variability overall, evidence of deeper within-state health inequality rather than just a higher average. Cancer and stroke rates were the exception, staying similar across both states, in line with the national finding that cancer doesn’t track poverty the way other conditions do.

title: Health and Poverty Across US Counties
text:
Clustering Counties Nationally
Correlation shows a relationship exists; clustering tests whether it is strong enough to sort counties into distinct groups without any labels attached. K-Means clustering was run on health outcomes and poverty, evaluated across k = 2 to 15 by silhouette score.


Visualization PCA Explained Variance Ratio (Health Outcomes): [0.66427219 0.17803825]









The best fit landed at just two clusters (silhouette = 0.379), the simplest possible split, but not a weak one. Cluster 0, lower-poverty counties, averaged a poverty rate of 11.15%, about 3.2 points below the roughly 14.4% national mean, and ran below average on nearly every outcome: 35.89% obesity, 9.79% diabetes, 29.83% high blood pressure, 12.88% total tooth loss. Cluster 1, higher-poverty counties, averaged 19.20% poverty, nearly 5 points above the mean, and ran above average across the board: 41.26% obesity, 13.18% diabetes, 21.22% tooth loss, 4.05% stroke prevalence. Cancer again broke from the pattern, showing no consistent separation between the two clusters, reinforcing that whatever drives its relationship to poverty isn’t the same mechanism driving every other condition.

title: Health and Poverty Across US Counties
text:
The Clearest Pattern: State-Level Clusters
The same clustering approach applied at the state level, rather than the county level, and repeated separately for health outcomes, risk behaviors, and racial breakdowns, produced the cleanest split of the entire analysis. Health-outcome clustering favored two groups (silhouette = 0.379), risk-behavior clustering favored two as well with a stronger fit (silhouette = 0.419), and racial-breakdown clustering favored two groups too, though with the weakest separation of the three (silhouette = 0.309), evidence that race adds less independent structure to the clustering than health outcomes or behavior do once poverty is already accounted for.









A hierarchical dendrogram of health outcomes and poverty made the same finding visually explicit. Hawaii and New Jersey broke off into their own cluster entirely, distinguished by exceptionally low poverty and strong health outcomes. At the other end, Mississippi, Louisiana, West Virginia, and Alabama grouped tightly together, sharing both high poverty and the worst health metrics in the dataset. A larger middle cluster, states like Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Colorado, and Iowa, sat between the two extremes with moderate poverty and comparatively balanced health profiles. A separate dendrogram built on risk behaviors alone reproduced nearly the same split: states like New Mexico, South Carolina, Georgia, and Oklahoma clustered around elevated smoking, inactivity, and poor sleep, while Maryland, Connecticut, New Jersey, and Hawaii clustered around healthier behavior patterns.

title: Health and Poverty Across US Counties
text:
Conclusion
Across every level of analysis tested, Michigan’s counties, the full national county dataset, and clustering at both the county and state level, poverty and health outcomes moved together. Poorer counties and states showed consistently worse rates of chronic disease, and unsupervised clustering, run without being told which counties were poor or healthy, converged on the same two groups every time. Hawaii and New Jersey stood out nationally as the healthiest, wealthiest cluster; high-poverty Southern states clustered tightly together on nearly every health metric tested. Cancer was the one consistent exception to an otherwise consistent pattern, a reminder that not every health outcome responds to poverty the same way, and that screening access and diagnostic patterns deserve their own investigation.

title: Health and Poverty Across US Counties
text:
Limitations
The CDC PLACES data is cross-sectional, a single year’s snapshot rather than a trend, and several measures are self-reported, which introduces reporting bias that could vary systematically with income or education. County-level aggregation also masks within-county disparities: a county’s average obscures how unevenly poverty and health can be distributed inside its own borders. And because health and poverty are correlated rather than experimentally manipulated, none of this establishes that poverty causes worse health outcomes, only that the two move together closely and consistently enough to be useful for identifying where public-health intervention might matter most.
